text: QAOA for ambulance, incident and hospital allocation

Opening: Our current quantum model selects dispatch assignments across incidents. OSRM provides journey times and road geometry. The experiment uses local noiseless Qiskit statevector simulation and compares QAOA samples with an exact classical baseline. We have not implemented a QUBO that selects individual road edges.

In OSRM mode, service.osrm_leg requests candidates and selects the minimum duration_s for each journey leg. It does not let QAOA choose the road edges within that leg. In synthetic mode, the code uses great-circle distances and a constant 30 km/h to estimate travel, drawing straight connectors. Road width, surface and vehicle clearance are not integrated into the allocation objective.

This numerical example illustrates the formula and is not a measured route result. The weighted objective is not the same as elapsed journey time, which would be 12 minutes in the example. The code filters unavailable ambulances, hospitals with no slots, and medical capability mismatches before computing choices. The unserved cost is severity times U, where U is one plus the sum of the maximum served cost in each incident group.

Exactly one choice is enforced per incident group. compatible() checks uniqueness of ambulance_id and hospital_id across served choices. Hospital.available_slots is currently restricted to zero or one. There is no multi-round scheduling or vehicle reuse over time. Unserved is a deliberate feasible outcome, with a large cost, rather than an invalid missing decision.

Q(x) = Σ cₖxₖ + P Σᵢ (1 − Σₖ∈Gᵢ xₖ)²
           + P Σ₍ₖ,ₗ₎∈F xₖxₗ
Gᵢ contains the retained choices for incident i
F contains choices for different incidents that share an ambulance or hospital

The code stores an upper-triangular Q matrix plus an offset. Expanding the one-choice square gives diagonal c_k−P, pair coefficient 2P for choices in the same incident group, and constant P per group. A conflicting pair across different incidents receives P once even if it shares both an ambulance and hospital. The stored penalty is one plus the sum of the maximum retained cost in each incident group. This formula represents the implementation, not the earlier planned edge-flow QUBO.

title: One qubit represents one candidate choice

text: One qubit represents one candidate choice

Ambulance A1 attends incident I2
and transports to hospital H3

Each retained Choice becomes one qubit in QuantumCircuit(n). The bit is a decision indicator, not a physical ambulance, hospital, road node or road segment. Measurement probabilities for a standalone qubit are |α|² and |β|². The full correlated multi-qubit state encodes probabilities over assignment combinations. No ambulance is dispatched by a superposition itself. The simulator returns classical samples that the backend decodes and validates.

Only 10 are valid in this illustration: nine served plans plus all unserved.

The blocks appear in application variable order. With one ambulance, at most one incident can be served in a single round. There are nine ways to pick one of three incidents and one of three hospitals, plus the all-unserved plan, assuming all nine served choices are eligible. The other 4,086 bitstrings violate one-choice or resource constraints. This example differs from the actual default scenario, which has three ambulances and medical capability filters. Qiskit raw bitstring display ordering may differ, so the implementation explicitly extracts bits using bit shifts indexed by qubit number.

Per incident: three cheapest

Shortlisting can remove the full optimum. The exact solver checks all eligible choices.

For the unfiltered 3×3×3 scenario the full choice count is 30 including unserved. build_problem retains group[:-1][:3] plus the unserved choice. At most three incidents times four retained choices gives 12 qubits. Direct calculation from demo_scenario with synthetic travel gives retained group sizes [3,3,4] for three hospitals, hence 10 qubits and 16 full choices. With five hospitals it gives [4,4,4], hence 12 qubits and 26 full choices. These are configuration counts, not benchmark outcomes.

Hcost = constant + Σ hₖZₖ + Σ JₖₗZₖZₗ
H prepares superposition. RZ/RZZ encode cost. RX mixes choices.

This is a schematic circuit fragment, not the complete transpiled circuit. The same RZZ interaction acts across a pair of choice qubits. The implementation converts diagonal QUBO terms into Z coefficients and off-diagonal terms into Z and ZZ coefficients. It applies RZ(2γh/scale), RZZ(2γJ/scale) and RX(2β), after Hadamard preparation. It divides Hamiltonian coefficients by a common scale while retaining the same relative objective. The diagram ends at statevector probabilities because the actual implementation samples a multinomial from those probabilities after optimization, rather than inserting hardware measurement instructions.

Expected QUBO cost
Sum of probability × cost
After tuning: sample the final distribution, then validate assignments.

At depth p the circuit has 2p adjustable angles. evaluate() builds a statevector and calculates an exact expectation from all basis-state probabilities. scipy.optimize.minimize uses COBYLA with the requested maxiter budget and a seeded initial point. The code keeps the best evaluated parameters, including when the optimizer exhausts its budget. Final sampling uses a seeded multinomial draw. Shots are final sample count, not repeated complete optimization runs. Current settings allow reps 1–3, shots 64–8192, and maxiter 10–100. No Aer or remote IBM hardware backend is currently used.

The service returns QAOA only when its valid sample matches
the full exact optimum within tolerance. Otherwise it uses the exact fallback.

service.allocate always computes the exact full-scenario and reduced-scenario optima. It validates quantum assignments again at the service boundary: one choice per incident, choices present in the model and no ambulance or hospital reuse. It selects QAOA only if candidate cost ≤ full optimum + 1e−8. A worse sample, unavailable dependencies or absent feasible sample triggers exact fallback. Therefore a good displayed final result alone is not evidence that QAOA found it. Inspect selected_solver, selection_reason and quantum.objective separately.

4,096 complex amplitudes. Our current application cap.
Over one billion amplitudes. About 16 GiB for the state alone.
The 12-qubit cap is a prototype choice, not a measured hardware limit.

Memory arithmetic assumes 16 bytes per complex128 amplitude: 2^30 × 16 bytes = 16 GiB. This is a statevector-only estimate, not a measurement of the laptop. Our implementation also stores basis indices, a bit matrix, energies and probabilities, so total memory is higher. Repeated circuit evaluation adds runtime. The code uses classical simulation on the laptop, not twelve physical qubits. Larger qubit counts and deeper circuits require resource profiling and possibly a different execution strategy.

Suggested demo narration: We first establish the travel-data source, then run QAOA plus the exact comparison. We inspect the QAOA candidate, whether it meets constraints, and why the application selected QAOA or classical fallback. Repeat with different seeds or settings before making a performance claim. A gap can arise from shortlisting or from QAOA search; compare full_exact_objective and reduced_exact_objective to distinguish these. No measured QAOA benchmark values are presented in this deck.

Close: The implemented quantum problem is joint emergency resource allocation. The earlier planned edge-selection routing formulation is separate future work. Current allocation costs use response time, severity and hospital transport time. Road-width, surface, clearance and live traffic are not yet integrated into that allocation model. The underlying route API can preserve available attributes separately. Operational dispatch would require authoritative data, field validation and approvals. The deck makes no claim of quantum speedup or real emergency suitability.
